reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: Vocal cord nodules are small, usually bilateral swellings on the vocal folds caused by chronic voice misuse or overuse
They typically sit at the junction of the anterior third and posterior two-thirds of the fold, the point of maximal contact during phonation
They are common in professional voice users, teachers, singers and habitually loud children
The main symptom is progressive hoarseness, often with vocal fatigue and a breathy quality, worse with use
On laryngoscopy early lesions look soft and reddish while long-standing nodules become firm, white and fibrotic
The mainstay of treatment is voice rest and speech therapy to correct the underlying vocal behaviour, which resolves most early nodules
Surgical excision (microlaryngoscopy) is reserved for mature fibrotic nodules that fail conservative treatment, and must be followed by voice therapy to prevent recurrence
Any hoarseness persisting beyond a few weeks, particularly in adults with risk factors, needs laryngeal examination to exclude malignancy
reference.pathophysiology: Vocal cord nodules form in response to repeated mechanical trauma from vocal abuse. Forceful or excessive vocal fold collision, especially at the midpoint of the membranous cord where impact stress is greatest, causes localised oedema and microhaemorrhage in the superficial lamina propria. With continued strain this reactive change organises into fibrosis and thickening of the overlying epithelium, producing symmetrical nodules on the medial edges of both folds. These masses prevent complete glottic closure and add mass to the vibrating edge, disrupting the mucosal wave and generating hoarseness and a breathy voice. Because both folds strike each other, lesions are characteristically bilateral and roughly symmetrical.
additionalDifferentials: Contact granuloma of the vocal process
additionalInvestigations: Laryngoscopy (flexible or rigid) to visualise the folds
Videostroboscopy to assess the mucosal wave and glottic closure
Voice assessment and acoustic analysis by a speech and language therapist
Biopsy of any atypical or suspicious lesion to exclude malignancy
Assessment for contributing factors such as reflux, allergy and vocal habits
redFlags: Persistent hoarseness beyond a few weeks in an adult, especially with smoking or alcohol use, requiring exclusion of malignancy
A unilateral, irregular or ulcerated lesion suggesting neoplasia rather than a nodule
Associated stridor, airway compromise or difficulty swallowing
Neck mass or referred otalgia accompanying the voice change
reference.prognosis: Early, soft nodules usually resolve completely with voice rest and speech therapy, and the outlook is excellent when vocal behaviour is corrected; mature fibrotic nodules may need surgery and, without behavioural change, nodules commonly recur.
pitfalls: Proceeding to surgery before an adequate trial of voice therapy
Mistaking a unilateral polyp, cyst or malignancy for benign nodules
Failing to arrange voice therapy after surgery, leading to recurrence
Ignoring persistent adult hoarseness that warrants cancer exclusion
Overlooking contributing factors such as reflux and ongoing vocal abuse
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Voice rest and speech and language therapy to correct the underlying vocal misuse, which resolves most early nodules
Vocal hygiene measures including hydration and avoidance of shouting and throat clearing to reduce vocal load
Address contributing factors such as reflux and allergy
Phonomicrosurgical excision reserved for mature, fibrotic nodules that fail conservative therapy
Ongoing voice-care and speech therapy to prevent recurrence after treatment
ENT referral with videostroboscopic monitoring of the folds
